questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of putting a message queue between a producer and a consumer?

options.text: It removes the need for the consumer to handle errors
It guarantees messages are processed in strict global order
It decouples them, so a slow or failed consumer does not block the producer
It compresses messages automatically

questions.explanation: The queue absorbs bursts and outages, letting each side scale and fail independently. Global ordering is usually the opposite — it is sacrificed once you partition the queue for throughput.

questions.prompt: Why is at-least-once delivery far more common than exactly-once in distributed messaging?

options.text: At-least-once guarantees strict ordering
Exactly-once needs coordination that is impossible to achieve end to end without idempotent consumers
At-least-once uses less network bandwidth
Exactly-once is only possible with UDP

questions.explanation: A broker cannot know whether a consumer crashed before or after processing, so it must redeliver. True exactly-once semantics come from making the consumer idempotent, not from the transport.

questions.prompt: What is a dead letter queue used for?

options.text: Holding messages that repeatedly fail processing, so they stop blocking the main queue
Prioritising messages from premium users
Buffering messages during a planned deployment
Storing messages that have been successfully processed

questions.explanation: Without one, a single poison message can be retried forever and stall everything behind it. Diverting it after a retry limit preserves throughput and leaves the failure available for inspection.

questions.prompt: What does the circuit breaker pattern protect against?

options.text: Unauthorised access to an internal service
Clock drift between servers
Repeatedly calling a failing dependency, wasting resources and delaying recovery
Data corruption during writes

questions.explanation: After a failure threshold the breaker opens and fails fast without calling the dependency, freeing threads and giving it room to recover. It periodically half-opens to test whether service has returned.

questions.prompt: Why should retries use exponential backoff with jitter rather than a fixed interval?

options.text: Fixed intervals synchronise clients into coordinated retry waves that re-overload the service
Exponential backoff guarantees the request eventually succeeds
Jitter reduces the total number of retries to one
Fixed intervals are not supported by HTTP

questions.explanation: Clients that fail together retry together, hammering a recovering service in lockstep. Growing delays reduce pressure and random jitter spreads the attempts out so they no longer arrive as a thundering herd.

questions.prompt: A token bucket rate limiter permits a burst above the sustained rate. What determines the maximum burst size?

options.text: The number of clients sharing the limiter
The rate at which tokens are refilled
The average request latency
The capacity of the bucket

questions.explanation: Tokens accumulate up to the bucket's capacity while traffic is idle, and a burst can consume all of them at once. The refill rate sets the long-run sustained throughput instead.

questions.prompt: What is backpressure in a streaming or pipeline system?

options.text: A downstream consumer signalling upstream to slow down when it cannot keep up
Replaying old messages to rebuild state
Compressing data before transmission
Rejecting requests from unauthenticated clients

questions.explanation: Without backpressure, a fast producer drives unbounded queue growth until memory is exhausted and the failure is catastrophic. Propagating the limit upstream converts that into controlled slowdown.

questions.prompt: Why does the bulkhead pattern isolate resources such as thread pools per dependency?

options.text: It reduces total memory usage across the service
One failing dependency cannot exhaust the resources needed by all the others
It guarantees each dependency responds within a fixed time
It allows dependencies to share a single connection

questions.explanation: With one shared pool, calls blocked on a slow dependency consume every thread and the entire service stops. Separate compartments confine the damage, exactly as bulkheads do in a ship's hull.

questions.prompt: In an event-driven architecture, what is the main advantage of publish-subscribe over point-to-point messaging?

options.text: It guarantees each message is delivered exactly once
It processes messages faster in every case
It removes the need for a message broker
New consumers can be added without changing the producer

questions.explanation: The producer emits an event without knowing who cares, so adding a consumer is a deployment rather than a code change upstream. The cost is that the flow of a request becomes harder to trace.

questions.prompt: What is graceful degradation in a service under heavy load?

options.text: Scaling automatically until the load is absorbed
Shedding or simplifying non-essential features so core functionality keeps working
Shutting the service down cleanly to protect data
Returning cached errors to every client

questions.explanation: Rather than failing entirely, the system drops recommendations, personalisation or analytics and keeps checkout working. This requires deciding in advance which features are expendable.
